t: Design Twitter — Timestamps, Follow Graphs, and K-Way Merge
o: We must simulate a mini social network: users post tweets, follow/unfollow each other, and query the 10 most recent tweets from themselves plus everyone they follow. The key observation is that tweets need a global ordering by recency — a monotonically increasing timestamp (or counter) assigned at post time gives us this for free. For `getNewsFeed`, we only care about the 10 newest tweets among all relevant users; since each user's own tweet list is already sorted newest-first (if we prepend), we can either collect and sort everything (simple) or do a k-way merge with a heap taking only the heads of each list (optimal). The small constraints (≤500 users, ≤3·10⁴ calls) mean even the brute force passes comfortably, but the heap approach is the expected 'design' answer. Walking through the example: user 1 posts tweet 5 → feed is [5]; after following user 2 who posts tweet 6, feed is [6,5] (newest first); unfollowing removes tweet 6, leaving [5]. Note a user always sees their own tweets regardless of follow state.
k: Assign each tweet a global increasing timestamp so recency comparisons are O(1).
Store each user's tweets newest-first (prepend or insert at head) so the front of every list is that user's most recent tweet.
getNewsFeed is a k-way merge of sorted lists: a min-heap of size k yields the top 10 in O(10 log k) instead of sorting all tweets.
A user's feed includes their own tweets even if they follow nobody.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force — Collect All Candidate Tweets and Sort
a.i: Keep one global list of (timestamp, tweetId, userId) plus a follow-set per user. On getNewsFeed, scan the entire global tweet list, keep tweets whose author is the user or someone they follow, sort descending by timestamp, and return the first 10 IDs. This is dead simple and correct; it just does unnecessary work scanning irrelevant tweets on every feed query.
s: Maintain a global array of [timestamp, tweetId, userId] with an incrementing clock, and a map userId -> set of followees.
postTweet appends to the global array.
follow/unfollow add/remove followeeId from followerId's set.
getNewsFeed filters the global array by author ∈ {userId} ∪ followees, sorts by timestamp descending, returns first 10 tweetIds.
a.t: O(T) per postTweet, O(T log T) per getNewsFeed where T is total tweets — filtering is linear, sorting dominates.
a.sp: O(T + F) for storing all tweets and follow relationships.

a.n: Approach 2: Per-User Tweet Lists + K-Way Heap Merge (Optimal)
a.i: Give each user their own tweet list stored newest-first (each tweet gets an increasing timestamp and we prepend). To build a feed, gather the head of each relevant user's list into a max-heap keyed by timestamp, then pop 10 times; each pop reveals that user's next-newest tweet, which we push back. This is exactly merging k sorted lists, touching only as many tweets as needed. Unfollowing simply excludes that user's list from the merge.
s: Keep Map<userId, List<[time, tweetId]>> with newest tweets inserted at index 0, and Map<userId, Set<followees>>.
postTweet: increment global time, prepend (time, tweetId) to the user's list.
getNewsFeed: seed a max-heap with the head entry of the user's list and each followee's list (store userId alongside so we can fetch the next element).
Pop up to 10 times: record tweetId, then push the next entry from that same user's list if any.
follow/unfollow just update the followee set.
a.t: postTweet O(L) due to list prepend (amortizable with a deque or append+reverse view); getNewsFeed O(k log k + 10 log k) where k is number of followed users — we only touch ~k+9 tweets.
a.sp: O(T + F) for all tweets and follow edges.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 to establish correctness quickly, then upgrade to the k-way heap merge — it demonstrates you recognize getNewsFeed as 'merge k sorted lists' and shows awareness that real systems avoid scanning all tweets. Common pitfalls: forgetting the user sees their **own** tweets without following themselves; using tweetId order instead of a timestamp (tweetIds are unique but not necessarily chronological); off-by-one when advancing a user's pointer after a heap pop; and unfollowing a user not currently followed (use discard/erase, which are safe no-ops). Edge cases: feeds with fewer than 10 tweets, repeated follow calls (sets dedupe naturally), and a user whose followee has zero tweets. Likely follow-ups: scale to millions of users (precomputed/push-based fan-out feeds vs pull-on-demand, pagination beyond 10, cache invalidation on unfollow), or support deleting tweets (lazy deletion via tombstones in the heap).
